title: The Bronte Sisters Publish as Men
text:
Charlotte, Emily and Anne Bronte grew up in the parsonage at Haworth, on the Yorkshire moors, with their father, a clergyman, and their brother Branwell. Their mother and two older sisters died when they were children. Shut in among the moors, the children invented imaginary kingdoms and wrote tiny books about them.

In the autumn of 1845, Charlotte came upon a notebook of Emily's poems. Emily was furious that her privacy had been invaded, but Charlotte was convinced the poems were remarkable, and Anne then shyly offered her own. In 1846 the three published a volume together, paying the costs themselves. They chose the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, keeping their own initials. Charlotte later explained that they did not want to be judged with the prejudice reserved for women writers. The book sold two copies.

They were not discouraged. Each had been writing a novel. In 1847 Charlotte's Jane Eyre became a sensation, and Emily's Wuthering Heights and Anne's Agnes Grey followed. Critics speculated that the Bells were one man. In 1848 Charlotte and Anne traveled to London to prove to their publisher that they were separate people.

Their success was short. Branwell died in September 1848, Emily in December, and Anne the following May. Charlotte's friend Elizabeth Gaskell told their story in her biography of 1857.
lesson: Siblings who believe in each other's talent can push one another past discouragement. A first failure is often only the first draft of a success.
people: Charlotte Bronte, Emily Bronte, Anne Bronte
source: Charlotte Bronte, Biographical Notice of Ellis and Acton Bell (1850); Elizabeth Gaskell, The Life of Charlotte Bronte (1857)
